content: 1. Selection or recall bias, particularly in self-reported outcomes, and the lack of control for confounding variables, were identified as limitations in the studies reviewed. 2. The systematic review highlighted key components that contribute to the success of breastfeeding promotion programs. These include group education combined with individual counseling sessions, addressing infant feeding counseling, involving fathers and family members, engaging community health workers or trained healthcare workers, and integrating PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission) programs with access to antiretroviral therapy. 3. Lisa Moloney and Deepa Handu contributed to the study by writing the protocol, screening citations, selecting and reviewing studies for inclusion, assessing study characteristics and risk of bias, and preparing the report. 4. In a study conducted in South Africa (Tomlinson, 2014), community health workers implemented structured home visiting programs aligned with PMTCT, Integrated Management of Childhood Illness, lactation counseling, and newborn care guidelines. Motivational interviewing techniques were used for breastfeeding counseling. Women received seven home visits, including two during pregnancy, one within 48 hours of delivery, and others at specific intervals postpartum. Low birth weight neonates received two additional visits in the first week. 5. In Zimbabwe (Piwowz, 2005), interventions included antenatal education on infant feeding in the context of HIV, male outreach and education, and counseling on infant feeding options for HIV-positive mothers. No intervention was provided to the control group. 6. In Malawi (Thakwalakwa, 2014), mothers were counseled on exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and supported with complementary feeding thereafter. There was no control group in this study. 7. In South Africa (Bland, 2008), women received antenatal counseling and up to three additional home visits to discuss feeding. Post-delivery, all women received one home visit within 72 hours, and breastfeeding mothers received further visits every two weeks for six months. The control group did not receive the scheduled number of visits. 8. In Zimbabwe (Iliff, 2005), study nurses were trained to counsel HIV-positive women on feeding options and optimal breastfeeding techniques to prevent complications such as cracked nipples and mastitis. The program emphasized exclusive breastfeeding for HIV-positive mothers who chose to breastfeed. No intervention was provided to the control group. 9. In India (Read, 2010), participants were referred to support groups for HIV and treatment centers. Infant feeding counseling was based on WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF training materials. Scheduled infant visits occurred at birth, one week, one month, and at regular intervals up to 12 months. The control group received standard care. 10. In Kenya (Bii, 2008), a cross-sectional study was conducted on a sample that had already undergone antenatal and postnatal counseling or education and was enrolled in PMTCT programs. No true intervention was conducted. 11. In Uganda (Matovu, 2008), a cross-sectional study involved a sample exposed to PMTCT interventions, including counseling or education. The study emphasized the importance of involving family members, especially fathers, in infant feeding counseling and education to improve adherence to exclusive breastfeeding. 12. In Cameroon (Nlend), group counseling sessions were conducted monthly during the antenatal period, focusing on sound breastfeeding practices. Trained nurses in lactation management and HIV, assisted by HIV-positive mothers who had successfully practiced exclusive breastfeeding, led the sessions. 13. In Tanzania (Young), counseling and education based on WHO/UNICEF/UNAIDS materials were provided during the antenatal and postnatal periods. The study highlighted the influence of male partner involvement and socioeconomic status on infant feeding decisions. 14. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) promotion has the potential to reduce postnatal HIV transmission among women unaware of their HIV status. Child survival and HIV prevention programs should support this practice. 15. Antiretroviral therapy provided to HIV-infected mothers who breastfed their infants resulted in over 90% HIV-free survival at six weeks of age. 16. Home visiting models by community health workers were found to be feasible and effective in promoting exclusive breastfeeding. Each additional visit by a community health worker was associated with a 6% relative increase in EBF rates. 17. Lay counselors were effective in promoting and sustaining exclusive breastfeeding among both HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. Community-wide promotion of EBF, rather than targeting only HIV-positive women, is recommended. 18. High-quality integrated PMTCT programs and maternal and newborn health (MNH) postnatal services are feasible and acceptable. These programs can promote early postnatal visits and improve care for both HIV-positive and HIV-negative mothers and their infants. 19. Cost-effective strategies are needed to improve breastfeeding practices among HIV-positive mothers. Group education combined with individualized counseling, frequent contact during antenatal and postnatal periods, and community involvement are critical to increasing EBF rates. 20. Education programs and infant feeding counseling significantly influence infant feeding choices and reduce breastfeeding-associated HIV transmission. These interventions should focus on safer breastfeeding practices and emphasize the benefits of EBF.
